verses.text: When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome, bought spices, that they might come and anoint him.
Very early on the first day of the week, they came to the tomb when the sun had risen.
They were saying among themselves, "Who will roll away the stone from the door of the tomb for us?"
for it was very big. Looking up, they saw that the stone was rolled back.
Entering into the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were amazed.
He said to them, "Don't be amazed. You seek Jesus, the Nazarene, who has been crucified. He has risen. He is not here. Behold, the place where they laid him!
But go, tell his disciples and Peter, 'He goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he said to you.'"
They went out,{TR adds "quickly"} and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had come on them. They said nothing to anyone; for they were afraid.
Now when he had risen early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons.
She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept.
When they heard that he was alive, and had been seen by her, they disbelieved.
After these things he was revealed in another form to two of them, as they walked, on their way into the country.
They went away and told it to the rest. They didn't believe them, either.

Afterward he was revealed to the eleven themselves as they sat at the table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they didn't believe those who had seen him after he had risen.
He said to them, "Go into all the world, and preach the Good News to the whole creation.
He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who disbelieves will be condemned.
These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak with new languages;
they will take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it will in no way hurt them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover."
So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was received up into heaven, and sat down at the right hand of God.
They went out, and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them, and confirming the word by the signs that followed. Amen.

items.label: M1
items.agent: Mary Magdalene, Mary mother of James, and Salome
items.outcome: spices in hand, with the intent to come and anoint him
items.narrator: anonymous third-person teller relating the women's actions
items.paraphrase: Once the rest-day had ended, the three named women purchased aromatic spices intending to go and dress the body.
items.gloss: This is love expressed as errand — the women act inside an ordinary practice of tending a body, doing what any mourner would do after the sabbath released them.
items.sitz: post-burial preparation practice among Jewish women following a sabbath-halted death
items.paradigm: corpse-care / anointing of the dead

items.label: M2
items.outcome: their arrival at the tomb at sunrise
items.narrator: same third-person teller, marking time and place
items.paraphrase: At daybreak on the week's first day they arrived at the burial place.
items.gloss: The arrival is still ordinary devotion; they come at first light because that is what mourners do, and the tomb is still, for them, a place with a body in it.
items.sitz: early-morning travel to a rock-cut tomb outside the city
items.paradigm: pilgrimage to a gravesite for mourning-rites

items.label: M3
items.outcome: the question uttered aloud among them
items.narrator: third-person teller reporting the women's own speech
items.paraphrase: As they walked they were voicing a worry to one another.
items.gloss: Their concern is practical rather than religious — an obstacle they can name to each other on the walk, not yet a mystery.
items.sitz: small group in transit, aware of the sealed tomb they are about to reach
items.paradigm: practical anticipation of an obstacle to the anointing

items.label: M4
items.substrate: the stone at the tomb's door
items.outcome: not-stated (open question, no answerer named)
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting their internal deliberation
items.paraphrase: They ask who will move the sealing-stone aside for them.
items.gloss: The worry surfaces as an actual question they can't answer among themselves — the errand runs into a limit their own hands cannot lift.
items.sitz: women physically incapable of shifting a large sealing-stone alone
items.paradigm: practical problem of gaining access to a sealed grave

items.label: M5
items.outcome: not-stated
items.narrator: third-person teller in editorial aside, warranting the women's worry
items.paraphrase: Aside from the narrator: the stone was of great size.
items.gloss: The teller steps aside to weight the barrier for us — we need to feel how heavy the stone is before we can feel what it means to find it moved.
items.sitz: teller flagging a physical fact readers need to feel the surprise of v.4b
items.paradigm: physical description of tomb architecture

items.label: M6
items.operation: see (that the stone was rolled back)
items.outcome: their perception that the stone is already moved
items.narrator: third-person teller reporting what the women visually apprehend
items.paraphrase: Raising their eyes, they perceived that the stone had already been shifted aside.
items.gloss: Their eyes register something that undoes the worry they were carrying — the very obstacle they had been rehearsing is already out of the way.
items.sitz: arrival at a tomb they expected to find sealed
items.paradigm: perception-as-discovery of an unexpected state

items.label: M7
items.outcome: the opening now unblocked
items.narrator: third-person teller, reporting the perceived state (agent of the rolling unspecified)
items.paraphrase: The stone had already been moved back from the opening.
items.gloss: The verb quietly leaves the doer unnamed — something greater than these women has already been at work here, and the text refuses to spell out by whom.
items.sitz: post-hoc discovery; the doer of the rolling is precisely what the text leaves open
items.paradigm: passive-divine / unnamed-agent state at a burial site

items.label: M8
items.operation: see (a young man sitting on the right, dressed in white)
items.substrate: M6a (the young man and his posture/attire)
items.outcome: their perception of an unexpected occupant
items.narrator: third-person teller reporting the women's discovery inside the tomb
items.paraphrase: Once inside the tomb, they saw a young figure seated to the right in a white robe.
items.gloss: Where they expected to meet a corpse they meet a living occupant — the tomb has stopped being a resting place and become an encounter.
items.sitz: entering a rock-cut tomb expecting a corpse and finding an unexpected living occupant
items.paradigm: encounter with a numinous/mediating figure at a threshold

items.label: M9
items.operation: sit (dressed in white, on the right)
items.agent: not-stated (the young man is a topic, not a doer here)
items.outcome: not-stated
items.narrator: third-person teller inside the women's perception
items.paraphrase: A young figure was seated on the right side, wearing a white robe.
items.gloss: The white robe and the right-hand seat signal without naming — the reader is being told, in the tradition's shorthand, that this is no ordinary young man.
items.sitz: the interior of the sealed tomb, occupied by a figure who should not be there
items.paradigm: white-clad seated messenger at a right-hand position — signaling status without naming it

items.label: M10
items.agent: not-stated (they undergo it, not perform it)
items.outcome: amazement as their state
items.narrator: third-person teller reporting the women's reaction
items.paraphrase: They were struck with astonishment.
items.gloss: Their fear is registered as its own datum — the encounter carries weight enough to shake them, and the text refuses to look away from that shaking.
items.sitz: reaction of ordinary mourners confronted with an inexplicable scene
items.paradigm: human awe/fear in the presence of a numinous figure

items.label: M11
items.outcome: his utterance directed at the women
items.narrator: third-person teller reporting the young man's speech
items.paraphrase: The young figure addressed them.
items.gloss: The figure takes the initiative — the frightened women do not have to find words first; speech comes toward them.
items.sitz: unnamed occupant of the tomb takes the initiative to speak to the frightened women
items.paradigm: messenger-announcement inside a sacred/liminal space

items.label: M12
items.outcome: an imperative to release the fear
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the young man
items.paraphrase: He orders them to stop being astonished.
items.gloss: His first word does something rather than merely says something — it releases them from the grip of the fear he has just walked into.
items.sitz: immediate pastoral response to the women's fright
items.paradigm: 'fear not' opening of a messenger-oracle

items.label: M13
items.operation: identify (whom you seek: Jesus the Nazarene, the crucified one)
items.outcome: the object of their search named as the crucified Nazarene
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the young man
items.paraphrase: He names whom they are looking for: the crucified Jesus of Nazareth.
items.gloss: He grounds the announcement in the specific dead man they came to tend — no vague apparition, but this particular crucified person.
items.sitz: the messenger anchors the announcement in the specific dead man whose body they came to tend
items.paradigm: identification of the addressed dead by name, origin, and manner of death

lineage.seam: Is the naming 'Jesus the Nazarene, the crucified one' standing on the Isaianic suffering-servant identification of the righteous one who is

items.label: M14
items.substrate: Jesus (as the one whose state is proclaimed)
items.outcome: the raising declared as accomplished; doer of the raising unnamed
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the young man's proclamation
items.paraphrase: He announces that the one they seek has been raised.
items.gloss: The very claim the community will hereafter confess is spoken here first — before any witness has seen him, the news is already in the air.
items.sitz: AD 70 hearers know 'has risen' as a claim that would ordinarily require witnesses; here the claim is delivered BEFORE any witness sees him
items.paradigm: resurrection-announcement whose agent (God) is left grammatically implicit

items.label: M15
items.outcome: not-stated
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the young man's negation
items.paraphrase: He denies that he is present in the tomb.
items.gloss: The absence itself is offered as the evidence — the empty place where he should be does the arguing.
items.sitz: the messenger removes the very body the women came to anoint from the frame of the tomb
items.paradigm: apophatic locative — the absence itself is the evidence

items.label: M16
items.operation: direct-attention (behold the place where they laid him)
items.outcome: the women's gaze turned to the vacated place as evidence
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the young man
items.paraphrase: He directs their attention to the spot where the body had been laid.
items.gloss: He points; the vacant slab is set before their own eyes to check — the claim is anchored to a spot they can look at.
items.sitz: the messenger anchors the announcement in a physical, checkable spot inside the tomb
items.paradigm: empty-place ostension — the vacancy is offered as attestation

items.label: M17
items.substrate: the women (as those to be dispatched)
items.outcome: an imperative to leave the tomb on an errand
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the young man
items.paraphrase: The messenger orders the women to depart.
items.gloss: The women stop being observers and become messengers — the encounter turns them outward, with an errand that is no longer their own.
items.sitz: messenger dispatching the only present witnesses onward with news
items.paradigm: commissioning of witnesses at a numinous site

items.label: M18
items.substrate: M10a (the message they are to convey)
items.outcome: the women charged to relay the message to the disciples and Peter
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the young man
items.paraphrase: He orders them to carry word to his followers, singling out Peter.
items.gloss: The news will travel only mouth-to-mouth, and Peter — who denied — is deliberately named back into the circle he had walked out of.
items.sitz: explicit inclusion of Peter marks him despite his prior denial as still addressed
items.paradigm: chain-of-witness commissioning; the empty tomb becomes news only through relay

items.label: M19
items.outcome: Jesus already en route to Galilee ahead of them
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the message the young man dictates
items.paraphrase: The message promises Jesus is going ahead of them to Galilee.
items.gloss: The reunion is relocated to home ground; the risen one goes on ahead as a shepherd goes on ahead, and the tomb is no longer where they will find him.
items.sitz: Galilee named as the reunion-site, not Jerusalem
items.paradigm: shepherd-going-before-flock; reunion relocated to the home country

lineage.seam: The young man's promise that Jesus 'goes before you into Galilee' repeats Jesus' own pre-Passion prediction, but leaves unsaid whether the m

items.label: M20
items.substrate: Jesus (as the one to be seen)
items.outcome: an encounter foretold in Galilee
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the message
items.paraphrase: The message promises they will see him there.
items.gloss: The seeing itself is set into a promise, not delivered here — the meeting is real, but it will happen elsewhere and later.
items.sitz: the announcement defers the risen-appearance from the tomb-site to Galilee
items.paradigm: future-tense witness-promise, not present-tense manifestation

items.label: M21
items.operation: recall prior saying (as he said to you)
items.outcome: the present promise warranted by Jesus' earlier words
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the young man's citation of Jesus
items.paraphrase: The message anchors itself in Jesus' prior speech to them.
items.gloss: The strange new thing is being read as fulfillment of an older word — what Jesus already said becomes the ground under what the messenger now announces.
items.sitz: the messenger presents the Galilee-appearance as fulfillment of something Jesus had already promised
items.paradigm: warrant-by-prior-word; new event legitimized by earlier prediction

lineage.seam: The clause 'as he said to you' explicitly anchors the present promise in Jesus' prior speech, but leaves unsaid the gap between a prediction

items.label: M22
items.outcome: the women away from the tomb
items.narrator: third-person teller reporting the women's departure
items.paraphrase: The women rushed out of the tomb in flight.
items.gloss: Whatever the messenger promised, their bodies react first — shock outruns the errand, and they leave before they have processed what they heard.
items.sitz: reaction of the just-commissioned witnesses, in the grip of shaking and shock
items.paradigm: flight from a numinous encounter

items.label: M23
items.substrate: the message they had just been given (M10a-c)
items.outcome: the commission un-executed; the news withheld
items.narrator: third-person teller reporting the women's non-speech
items.paraphrase: They kept silent, telling no one anything.
items.gloss: The commission was given and it did not travel — the very first witnesses fall silent exactly where they were told to speak, and the account refuses to smooth the paradox over.
items.sitz: the AD 70 hearer, who KNOWS the resurrection was somehow proclaimed, meets the paradox that the first commissioned witnesses said nothing
items.paradigm: failed-commission / suppressed announcement

items.label: M24
items.operation: rise (early on the first day of the week)
items.agent: Jesus (as the one risen; the raiser unnamed)
items.outcome: Jesus alive at daybreak of the first day
items.narrator: third-person teller (a later editorial voice; the pericope shifts register here)
items.paraphrase: He had been raised early on the week's first day.
items.gloss: What the messenger had announced is now restated in the community's own confessing voice — the resurrection is spoken of as an accomplished fact, no longer only reported at a tomb.
items.sitz: later scribal summary re-narrating the raising as background before the appearance-list
items.paradigm: resurrection-as-accomplished-event, without depicted raising

lineage.seam: Is the temporal marker 'early on the first day of the week' for the rising standing on the Hoseanic 'on the third day he will raise us up,'

items.label: M25
items.substrate: Mary Magdalene (as recipient of the appearance)
items.outcome: Mary Magdalene as the first to see him alive
items.narrator: third-person teller listing appearances
items.paraphrase: He showed himself first to Mary Magdalene, previously freed by him of seven demons.
items.gloss: The account catalogs whom he showed himself to and ranks Mary first — priority of witness is being asserted, not just narrated.
items.sitz: later teller ranks Mary Magdalene as first witness — priority is asserted
items.paradigm: appearance-list; the risen one initiates contact with a named recipient

lineage.seam: The parenthetical 'from whom he had cast out seven demons' imports Mary Magdalene's back-story as established fact, but leaves unsaid whethe

items.label: M26
items.operation: go (to those who had been with him)
items.substrate: the former companions of Jesus (as those approached)
items.outcome: Mary arriving among the disciples
items.narrator: third-person teller
items.paraphrase: She set out to those who had been Jesus' companions.
items.gloss: Where the earlier women fled and kept silent, she carries the errand — the failed relay is being redone by a named witness.
items.sitz: unlike the women in v.8, Mary executes the errand
items.paradigm: witness-relay initiated by the first appearance-recipient

items.label: M27
items.substrate: the appearance she had received (M14, opaque in the text)
items.outcome: the disciples informed by her testimony
items.narrator: third-person teller
items.paraphrase: She reported to them what had happened.
items.gloss: A woman is the first mouth to carry the resurrection to the men — the chain of witness begins in earnest, on her word.
items.sitz: first attested resurrection-testimony delivered by a woman to the male disciples
items.paradigm: witness-relay; the appearance is now propagated by report

items.label: M28
items.operation: hear (that he was alive and had been seen by her)
items.outcome: the report received by them
items.narrator: third-person teller
items.paraphrase: They took in the news that he was alive and that she had seen him.
items.gloss: The message arrives at its recipients — but the text quietly separates hearing from believing, and lets the gap between them stand.
items.sitz: the message reaches its recipients, testing whether relay = belief
items.paradigm: reception-of-testimony as a distinct step from reception-of-truth

items.label: M29
items.outcome: not-stated
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the content of Mary's report as heard
items.paraphrase: The reported content: he is alive.
items.gloss: Underneath all the reporting sits the bare claim — that this particular dead man is alive — and here it is stated in that stripped-down form.
items.sitz: the core proposition the AD 70 hearer is asked to receive
items.paradigm: resurrection-as-present-state, predicated of the dead one

items.label: M30
items.outcome: Mary's eyewitness status established in the report
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the report's second clause
items.paraphrase: And: he had been seen by her.
items.gloss: Her having-seen is offered as the ground under the claim — the assertion rests on a named person's eyes, not on rumor.
items.sitz: eyewitness credential offered as warrant for the state-claim in M17a
items.paradigm: seeing-by-a-named-witness as evidentiary basis

items.label: M31
items.outcome: the testimony rejected
items.narrator: third-person teller
items.paraphrase: They refused to credit it.
items.gloss: The relay hits a wall — hearing does not compel belief, and the teller marks this refusal squarely rather than covering it.
items.sitz: AD 70 teller flags the disciples' initial disbelief as a pattern, not an anomaly
items.paradigm: testimony-rejection; hearing does not yet compel belief

items.label: M32
items.operation: appear (in another form, to two of them)
items.outcome: a second appearance, in altered form, to two named-by-role recipients
items.narrator: third-person teller continuing the appearance-list
items.paraphrase: Later he showed himself in a different guise to two of them as they were walking out to the countryside.
items.gloss: He is recognizable but altered — the same one and not the same — and the account lets that strangeness stand as a feature of how he now shows himself.
items.sitz: later teller catalogs multiple appearances, marking altered-form as a feature
items.paradigm: appearance-list; risen-Jesus recognizable yet other

lineage.seam: The brief notice that Jesus appeared 'in another form to two of them as they walked into the country' compresses the Emmaus episode into a s

items.label: M33
items.substrate: the rest of the group (as those approached)
items.outcome: the two arriving back among the others
items.narrator: third-person teller
items.paraphrase: The two set off back to the others.
items.gloss: Like Mary before them, the two turn back with what they have seen — the pattern of relay repeats with a second pair of witnesses.
items.sitz: second witness-relay attempt, parallel to Mary's
items.paradigm: witness-relay initiated by appearance-recipients

items.label: M34
items.outcome: the rest informed by their testimony
items.narrator: third-person teller
items.paraphrase: They reported what had happened to the others.
items.gloss: Another set of eyewitnesses passes the news to the group — the pattern that began with Mary is happening again on wider ground.
items.sitz: second witness-relay to the wider group
items.paradigm: propagation of an appearance-report

items.label: M35
items.outcome: the second testimony also rejected
items.narrator: third-person teller marking the pattern as repeated
items.paraphrase: The rest again refused to credit them.
items.gloss: Disbelief is not a one-time failure but a repeating pattern — even a second eyewitness report is turned away, and the teller wants us to feel that repetition.
items.sitz: the teller drives home a repeated pattern of disbelief across independent witnesses
items.paradigm: testimony-rejection as a recurring baseline in the resurrection-report chain

items.label: M36
items.substrate: the eleven (as recipients of the appearance)
items.outcome: the whole remaining core-group as first-hand recipients at last
items.narrator: third-person teller closing the appearance-list with the full group
items.paraphrase: Later he showed himself to the eleven while they were reclining at a meal.
items.gloss: When relay fails, he shows himself directly — the deadlock of unbelief is finally broken not by better witnesses but by his own coming.
items.sitz: AD 70 teller resolves the failed-relay pattern by having Jesus appear directly to the whole eleven
items.paradigm: table-appearance to the whole apostolic group

lineage.seam: The appearance 'to the eleven as they sat at table' condenses the Lukan/Johannine table-appearance to the gathered disciples, but leaves uns

items.label: M37
items.operation: rebuke (them for their unbelief and hardness of heart)
items.substrate: the eleven's unbelief (M18, M22) and hardness of heart
items.outcome: their prior disbelief named and censured
items.narrator: third-person teller
items.paraphrase: He reproached them for refusing to trust the earlier witnesses and for their obdurate hearts.
items.gloss: He does not spare them — their refusal to trust the witnesses is named as a fault they must own before they are sent anywhere.
items.sitz: the teller stages a formal reckoning with the disbelief pattern he has just narrated
items.paradigm: rebuke of hardened hearts by the risen one himself

items.label: M38
items.outcome: the commission and its accompanying promises delivered
items.narrator: third-person teller framing the risen one's speech
items.paraphrase: He addressed them with a commissioning speech.
items.gloss: The rebuke gives way to a fresh address — what he says next will carry the weight of a final charge, and the account slows to frame it.
items.sitz: AD 70 teller places the universal-mission mandate in the risen one's own mouth
items.paradigm: post-resurrection dominical commission

items.label: M39
items.outcome: the eleven charged with a worldwide errand
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the commission
items.paraphrase: He orders them to travel throughout the whole world.
items.gloss: The circle is torn open — the whole world becomes the field, and their sending is no longer limited to their own people.
items.sitz: an outward commission to 'all the world' is imaginable to an AD 70 teller writing after the Pauline mission has already gone across the empire
items.paradigm: sending-out beyond the ethnic boundary

lineage.seam: 'Go into all the world' echoes the Matthean 'go therefore,' but leaves unsaid whether the geographic-universal frame ('all the world') is a

items.label: M40
items.operation: command (preach the good news to the whole creation)
items.substrate: the whole creation (as the audience of proclamation)
items.outcome: the eleven charged with universal proclamation
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the commission
items.paraphrase: He orders them to proclaim the good news to every creature.
items.gloss: The mandate widens beyond even the human circle — the news is to be spoken toward the whole of what has been made.
items.sitz: 'good news to the whole creation' as an emerging phrase for the post-Jewish-war mission horizon
items.paradigm: universal proclamation, addressed beyond the human circle

lineage.seam: The universal commission 'go into all the world and preach the good news to the whole creation' rhymes with the Matthean Great Commission's

items.label: M41
items.agent: the risen Jesus (as promiser); God (as implicit saver)
items.outcome: salvation for the believer-and-baptized
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the promise
items.paraphrase: He promises that whoever trusts the proclamation and is initiated by washing will be delivered.
items.gloss: Salvation is offered on terms the community can recognize — trust in the message and the washing that marks initiation into it.
items.sitz: AD 70 community already practicing baptismal initiation gates salvation-claim by that rite
items.paradigm: conditional salvation-formula riding on belief plus initiation-rite

items.label: M42
items.agent: the risen Jesus (as warner); God (as implicit judge)
items.outcome: condemnation for the disbeliever
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the counterpart warning
items.paraphrase: He warns that whoever refuses to trust will be sentenced against.
items.gloss: The other side of the gate is spelled out — refusing to trust is named as a stance with judicial weight, not a neutral withholding.
items.sitz: the same community frames disbelief as a stance with judicial consequence
items.paradigm: binary salvation/condemnation gate, keyed on belief

lineage.seam: Is the binary 'whoever disbelieves will be condemned' standing on the Johannine judgment-formula in which the one who does not believe is al

items.label: M43
items.outcome: a set of accompanying signs guaranteed to attend them
items.narrator: third-person teller
items.paraphrase: He promises that a set of signs will attend those who trust the proclamation.
items.gloss: Those who trust will not walk unattended — the community catalogs the signs by which its confession will be known and confirmed.
items.sitz: post-70 community with charismatic phenomena in circulation catalogues them here
items.paradigm: sign-attestation of the believing community

items.label: M44
items.outcome: demons expelled under the invoked name of Jesus
items.narrator: third-person teller quoting the enumerated sign
items.paraphrase: In his name they will expel demons.
items.gloss: His name becomes the very means of the authority — his followers act by invoking him, not out of any strength of their own.
items.sitz: exorcism-in-Jesus'-name already an attested practice in the AD 70 mission field
items.paradigm: authority-by-invoked-name

items.label: M45
items.outcome: speech in tongues they had not known
items.narrator: third-person teller
items.paraphrase: They will speak in new tongues.
items.gloss: New speech will pour out of them — a spirit-borne fluency the community already knows in its own gatherings.
items.sitz: tongues-phenomenon known to Pauline and post-Pauline communities
items.paradigm: charismatic speech as sign

cells.seam: Is the naming 'Jesus the Nazarene, the crucified one' standing on the Isaianic suffering-servant identification of the righteous one who is 'cut off,' and if so does the messenger's identification-through-crucifixion preserve the servant's vindication-after-suffering pattern or reassign it to a single named figure?

The young man's promise that Jesus 'goes before you into Galilee' repeats Jesus' own pre-Passion prediction, but leaves unsaid whether the messenger's warrant derives from having heard Jesus or from independent angelic knowledge — the identity of source-sense (Jesus' prediction of post-resurrection reunion) and use-sense (fulfillment-announcement) is asserted by the 'as he told you' formula without accounting for how the messenger knows.

The clause 'as he said to you' explicitly anchors the present promise in Jesus' prior speech, but leaves unsaid the gap between a prediction spoken only to the disciples (not to the women) and its being relayed BY the women — the chain of transmission is asserted but not narrated.

Is the temporal marker 'early on the first day of the week' for the rising standing on the Hoseanic 'on the third day he will raise us up,' and if so does the shift from a communal covenant-restoration idiom to a single figure's dawn-resurrection preserve or reassign the source's sense?

The parenthetical 'from whom he had cast out seven demons' imports Mary Magdalene's back-story as established fact, but leaves unsaid whether the appended verses are drawing on Luke's tradition or on a shared pre-gospel notice — the identification is used to authorize her as first witness without narrating how the reader is expected to know it.

The brief notice that Jesus appeared 'in another form to two of them as they walked into the country' compresses the Emmaus episode into a summary, but leaves unsaid whether 'another form' is the compiler's own interpretation of the Lukan non-recognition motif or an independent tradition — the borrowing repackages a full narrative as a datum in a disbelief-sequence.

The appearance 'to the eleven as they sat at table' condenses the Lukan/Johannine table-appearance to the gathered disciples, but leaves unsaid whether the meal-setting is retained for its Lukan force (bodily eating as proof) or merely as a scene-marker — the borrowing keeps the setting while dropping the demonstration.

'Go into all the world' echoes the Matthean 'go therefore,' but leaves unsaid whether the geographic-universal frame ('all the world') is a fresh coinage or a re-cast of the Matthean ethnic-universal ('all nations').

The universal commission 'go into all the world and preach the good news to the whole creation' rhymes with the Matthean Great Commission's 'all nations,' but leaves unsaid whether 'whole creation' preserves the Matthean ethnic-universal sense or extends it cosmically — the borrowing enlarges the audience while retaining the commissioning form.

Is the binary 'whoever disbelieves will be condemned' standing on the Johannine judgment-formula in which the one who does not believe is already condemned, and if so does it preserve realized-condemnation or shift it into future-verdict?

The promise that believers 'will speak in new tongues' rhymes with the Pentecost narrative of the disciples speaking in other languages, but leaves unsaid whether 'new' preserves the Lukan sense of previously-unknown human languages given for cross-cultural proclamation or extends it toward a broader charismatic-speech phenomenon.

Is the promise 'they will take up serpents' standing on the Malta episode where Paul shakes off a viper unharmed, and if so does the borrowing generalize a one-time apostolic sign into a standing believer-charism?

The promise of hand-laying healing rhymes with apostolic healing practice, but leaves unsaid whether the gesture preserves the apostolic-office frame or extends the charism to every believer without distinction.

Is the notice that the Lord 'was received up into heaven' standing on the Elijah ascent, and if so does it preserve the prophet-taken-alive pattern or repurpose it as post-resurrection enthronement rather than escape from death?

The being-taken-up rhymes with the Lukan ascension notices, but leaves unsaid whether the borrowing preserves Luke's carefully-narrated ascension-scene or condenses it into a bare theological datum stripped of setting and witnesses.

'Sat down at the right hand of God' imports the royal-oracle image of the Davidic lord seated at YHWH's right, but leaves unsaid whether the enthronement's original sense — a king awaiting the subjection of enemies — is preserved as ongoing wait or collapsed into an accomplished vindication.

Is the notice that the Lord confirmed the word by accompanying signs standing on the Hebrews formula that God bore witness to the message by signs and wonders, and if so does the borrowing preserve God-as-attester or reassign the attesting to the risen Lord?

glossa.source_pressure: The Greek verb is ἠγέρθη — a MARKED aorist passive (the passivum divinum, God the unspoken agent). Mark had active options (ἤγειρεν 'he raised him', ἀνέστη 'he rose'), so the passive was a choice, not a necessity.
glossa.rendering_choice: Each version decides what to do with a theological load already on the verb: Latin surrexit (ACTIVE — partly language-forced, resurgo has no passive); KJV 'is risen' (stative be-perfect); WEB 'has risen' (eventive have-perfect).
glossa.formal_consequence: A passive → active → stative → eventive drift; and the announcement fuses to one move in Latin, atomizes to four in the KJV.
glossa.interpretive_stakes: God's act (passive) vs Jesus's own act (active) — but the theology is MARK's, encoded in the 1st-century Greek, not the translators'. They inherit the load and decide what to carry.
glossa.citation: Thayer s.v. ἐγείρω; Lewis & Short s.v. resurgo; panel verdict (RESITUATE_translation_panel_pilot_readable_s161)

reception.title: The resurrection end-silence — how it was received

readers.label: Lake
readers.reading: Lake treats the women's silence as the deliberate, emphatic main point of Mark's ending, while allowing that a now-lost continuation likely explained how they eventually spoke.
readers.quoted_span: the deliberate silence of the women at the beginning — which is the main point — is perfectly plain, for the statement is quite emphatic

readers.label: Orr (1908)
readers.reading: Orr acknowledges Mark breaks off at the women's flight in trembling, but insists Mark's Gospel nonetheless implied — no less than the others — that a report followed.
readers.quoted_span: St. Mark breaks off with the women fleeing from the tomb in "trembling and astonishment" ; but there can be no reasonable doubt that his Gospel also, not less than the others, contemplated a report of t

readers.label: Mark · ICC
readers.reading: Gould normalizes the abrupt ending as consistent with Mark's habitual brevity at the gospel's margins — not strange, not requiring explanation, simply characteristic.
readers.quoted_span: Mark gives merely the announcement of the resurrection to the women by the angels, and closes with this. This, instead of being strange, and requiring explanation, is quite in accordance with the character of Mark

readers.label: Matthew · ICC
readers.reading: Allen reads Mark's silence as naturally inviting a follow-up appearance; Matthew, uneasy with it, rewrites the women as speaking, then continues with the appearance — but unmotivated.
readers.quoted_span: It is very natural that this should have been followed by an appearance to them of Christ dispelling their fear and repeating the angel's message. Mt. alters "and told no one," etc., into "ran to tell His disciples."

readers.label: Longer Ending (16:9–20)
readers.reading: The most consequential reception act: a later hand SUPPLIED an ending — appearances + commission + ascension — precisely because Mark's abrupt 16:8 silence was felt as a gap that had to be closed.

readers.label: Shorter Ending
readers.reading: A second, briefer supplied ending in some manuscripts — independent evidence that the 16:8 silence generated MULTIPLE closure-attempts, not one.

readers.label: Narrative criticism
readers.reading: Reads 16:8 not as a defect or accident but as an INTENTIONAL narrative choice — the silence forces the reader to supply the continuation (the 'hermeneutic of secrecy'). NOT in our corpus (the narrative-critical register is a known coverage gap, IRR228) — added as attested/inferred.

center.label: Mark 16:8 — the end-silence
center.reading: Each account ends on a silence; Mark breaks off abruptly with the women afraid and saying nothing. What happens after is unnarrated, later supplied, or left open — the meaty end-gap.
center.title: The resurrection end-silence (Mark 16:8 · the unnarrated after)

beats.note: lightning/snow (MATT), white robe (MARK), dazzling clothes (LUKE), white (JOHN)

beats.beat: the witnesses react with fear, dread, or bewilderment
beats.note: MATT guards struck down + women's mingled fear/joy; MARK alarm/terror; LUKE terror + bowing; JOHN grief rather than terror

beats.beat: the figure(s) address the witnesses with a speech-act interpreting the empty tomb
beats.note: MATT/MARK a commission; LUKE a rhetorical rebuke + reminder; JOHN only a 'why do you weep' question

beats.beat: the sought one is identified as the crucified Jesus
beats.note: MATT/MARK by the angelic naming, LUKE embedded in the passion-prediction; JOHN never verbalizes crucifixion in this scene

beats.beat: his absence from the tomb is explicitly declared ('he is not here')
beats.note: formulaic in the synoptics; JOHN dramatizes absence but never states the formula

beats.beat: his resurrected/raised status is announced (typically as divine passive)
beats.note: MATT/MARK/LUKE via the figures' proclamation; JOHN gestures at it only through the beloved disciple's belief and a scriptural aside

beats.beat: the witnesses are invited to view/verify the vacated burial spot
beats.note: MATT/MARK by directive ('come, see'); LUKE by finding no body; JOHN by inspection of the linen wrappings

beats.beat: a prior word of Jesus is invoked to frame what has happened
beats.note: MATT/MARK cite his earlier promise about Galilee; LUKE cites the passion-and-resurrection prediction; JOHN cites scripture instead

beats.beat: the witnesses depart from the tomb
beats.note: MATT hasten with fear+joy; MARK flee in terror; LUKE return to the eleven; JOHN Mary runs to Peter, disciples return home

beats.beat: the witnesses are commissioned/moved to report to the (male) disciples
beats.note: explicit commission in MATT/MARK; LUKE self-initiated report; JOHN Mary's spontaneous run to Peter/beloved disciple

beats.beat: the announcement is (or is to be) carried to Peter and the wider disciple circle
beats.note: MARK names Peter in the commission (and shorter ending); LUKE the eleven; JOHN Peter and the beloved disciple; MATT names 'his disciples' without Peter

beats.beat: a promise of future seeing/reunion with the risen Jesus is issued
beats.note: both locate it in Galilee via a 'he goes before you' formula; absent from LUKE and JOHN's tomb scene

beats.beat: male disciple(s) go to the tomb to verify the women's report
beats.note: LUKE Peter alone; JOHN Peter with the beloved disciple in a footrace

beats.beat: the linen burial cloths are seen lying in the tomb
beats.note: LUKE a single mention by Peter; JOHN elaborated as wrappings plus separately rolled head-cloth

beats.beat: a closing cognitive/affective state is left unresolved into full belief
beats.note: MARK women's fearful silence; LUKE Peter's amazement; contrast JOHN's beloved-disciple belief and MATT's commissioned joy

absence.status: Method S180 ruled: the open ring carries EPISTEMIC STATUS only; the KIND of absence is a SECOND, orthogonal encoding (RULING 1). Five kinds have live stores; four gap-id namespaces still lack a crosswalk and two of them reach no deployed feed, so only the kind this slice can actually resolve is rendered.

typed_now.claim: a move that stands on no source — most do not stand on one; that is correct, not missing data

not_an_absence.ruling: The text SAYS the women said nothing. That is something the writer put there — not something our reading failed to find. So it is not counted here as a gap at all; it is one of the things the passage does, and it is marked as one.
not_an_absence.shown_as: move M23 (say nothing), in the SEE lens

awaiting_reader: one shared way of naming a gap, so a gap seen in one reading can be looked up in another

reliability.disposition: Reliability for this reading: not established. 1 of 11 engines has been measured, and no acceptance threshold has been declared — so the measurement cannot yield a verdict.
reliability.why_no_number: A number with no acceptance criterion cannot produce a verdict, and drawing it beside a claim will read as one. Repetition is evidence that runs happened, not that they agreed; agreement between runs is evidence about the instrument's stability, not about whether the reading is right.
reliability.not_rendered_on_the_page: the agreement figures above -- deliberately (see why_no_number)
